docs.title: 8. PPM RC Receiver Input & Bidirectional DShot ESC Output (syn_ppm.h, syn_dshot.h, syn_dshot_telemetry.h)
docs.text:
• PPM Multi-Channel Decoder (input/syn_ppm.h, SYN_USE_PPM): SYN_PPM_Decoder (syn_ppm_init, syn_ppm_process_pulse, syn_ppm_get_channel) decodes timer input-capture pulse widths (> 2700 us sync gap) into up to 12 1000..2000 us RC receiver channels.
  • Digital ESC DShot Frame Encoder (output/syn_dshot.h, SYN_USE_DSHOT): syn_dshot_encode(throttle, telemetry, &pkt) and syn_dshot_us_to_throttle(us) pack 11-bit throttle commands (0..2047), telemetry request bits, and 4-bit nibble-XOR CRCs into 16-bit DShot150/300/600 frames (SYN_DShot_Packet).
  • Bidirectional DShot GCR Telemetry (output/syn_dshot_telemetry.h, SYN_USE_DSHOT_TELEMETRY): syn_dshot_decode_gcr_20bit() and syn_dshot_parse_telemetry() decode 20-bit GCR (5b/4b) ESC responses, verify CRC, and compute commutation period (us), eRPM, and mechanical RPM (SYN_DShot_Telemetry).

docs.title: Cooperative Multitasking
docs.text: SyntropicOS provides a cooperative multitasking kernel built on protothreads — stackless coroutines where standalone SYN_PT continuation state costs 2 bytes of RAM (uint16_t lc), and full scheduled SYN_Task descriptors with priority, delays, mutex tracking, and event-blocking cost 44 bytes per task descriptor on 32-bit targets (80 bytes on 64-bit LP64 targets, with zero per-task stack allocation).

docs.title: Protothreads
docs.text:
Module Header Config Protothreads pt/syn_pt.h SYN_USE_PT Semaphores pt/syn_pt_sem.h SYN_USE_PT

Protothreads are stackless cooperative coroutines implemented via the Duff's device trick (switch/__LINE__ continuation). Each SYN_PT struct is a single uint16_t.

Core macros:

Macro Description PT_BEGIN(pt) Open a protothread body (must be first) PT_END(pt) Close body and return PT_ENDED (normal completion) PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, cond) Yield PT_IDLE until condition is true PT_WAIT_WHILE(pt, cond) Yield PT_IDLE while condition is true PT_PASS(pt) Yield PT_IDLE — no immediate work; let other ready tasks run this round PT_CONTINUE(pt) Yield PT_MORE — completed a work chunk and more work is waiting PT_CONTINUE_IF_NEEDED(pt, task) Yield PT_MORE only if syn_task_should_share(task) is true (sched/syn_sched.h) PT_EXIT(pt) Abort immediately and return PT_EXITED PT_RESTART(pt) Reset continuation and return PT_IDLE PT_SPAWN(pt, child, func) Run child protothread until exit, propagating child PT_IDLE / PT_MORE verbatim PT_DELAY_MS(pt, target, ms) Non-blocking delay (needs a uint32_t* for deadline storage) PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, ms) Convenience form using task->delay_until PT_BLOCK_CONDITION(pt, task, cond) Park task in SYN_TASK_BLOCKED without polling while cond is false; requires explicit syn_task_resume(task) from an ISR/driver/producer to re-evaluate cond PT_BLOCK_EVENT(pt, task, grp, mask) Block task execution (SYN_TASK_BLOCKED) until event bit fires PT_BLOCK_EVENT_WITH_TIMEOUT(pt, task, grp, mask, ms, out) Block task execution (SYN_TASK_BLOCKED) until event bit fires OR timeout elapses

docs.title: Macro Expansion Under the Hood (Duff's Device)
docs.text:
Protothreads save execution position using a 2-byte line continuation variable (uint16_t lc) and C switch/case jump tables:

High-Level C CodePreprocessor Macro Expansion 
SYN_PT_Status blink_task(SYN_PT *pt)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    while (1) {
        HAL_GPIO_TogglePin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_5);
        PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, (syn_port_get_tick_ms() - last_tick) >= 500);
        last_tick = syn_port_get_tick_ms();
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

SYN_PT_Status blink_task(SYN_PT *pt)
{
    char _pt_yield_flag = 1;
    switch (pt->lc) {
        case 0:
            while (1) {
                HAL_GPIO_TogglePin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_5);

                /* PT_WAIT_UNTIL expansion: saves __LINE__ (10) into pt->lc before returning.
                 * On next function invocation, switch(pt->lc) jumps directly to 'case 10:' 
                 * inside the while loop, bypassing function re-entry and resuming execution! */
                pt->lc = 10; case 10:
                if (!((syn_port_get_tick_ms() - last_tick) >= 500)) {
                    return PT_IDLE;
                }

                last_tick = syn_port_get_tick_ms();
            }
    }
    _pt_yield_flag = 0;
    pt->lc = 0;
    return PT_ENDED;
}

docs.title: Writing Tasks: Rules and Gotchas
docs.text: Protothreads use a switch/__LINE__ continuation technique (sometimes called Duff's device). This is invisible in normal use, but it creates two constraints you must follow.

docs.title: Rule 1: Local variables don't survive across yields or delays
docs.text:
When a task hits PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(), PT_PASS(), PT_CONTINUE(), or any PT_WAIT_* macro, it returns from the function. When the scheduler calls it again, execution resumes at the saved line — but local variables on the stack are gone.

// ❌ BAD: 'count' resets every time the task resumes
static SYN_PT_Status counter_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        int count = 0;                          // Allocated on the stack
        count++;
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 1000);       // Task returns here → stack is gone
        // 'count' is undefined after this point
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

Fix: Use static locals, file-scope globals, or task->user_data:

// ✅ Option A: static local
static SYN_PT_Status counter_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    static int count = 0;    // Lives in .bss, survives across yields
    for (;;) {
        count++;
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 1000);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// ✅ Option B: user_data pointer (best for multiple task instances)
static SYN_PT_Status counter_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    int *count = (int *)task->user_data;
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        (*count)++;
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 1000);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

Local Variables & Resumption

Because protothreads are stackless and resume execution using a switch statement under the hood, automatic local variables do not preserve their state across a yield.

  • Across a Yield: Any variable whose value must survive a yield (PT_PASS, PT_CONTINUE, PT_WAIT_UNTIL, etc.) must be declared static or stored in a persistent structure (like user_data).
  • Before PT_BEGIN: Declaring a local variable before PT_BEGIN does not make it safe to use across a yield. Its declaration code will re-run on every invocation, resetting the variable to its initial value.
  • Between Yields: Local variables are only safe if their entire usage is self-contained between two consecutive yield points. To avoid compiler warnings about jumping over variable initializations, declare them inside a nested block { ... } between the yields, or declare them before PT_BEGIN (if they do not need to persist across yields).

docs.title: Rule 2: No switch statements inside a protothread body
docs.text:
Because PT_BEGIN/PT_END expand to a switch/case construct, placing your own switch inside the protothread body produces nested switch labels that confuse the compiler.

// ❌ BAD: compiler error — nested switch conflicts with PT macros
static SYN_PT_Status my_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        switch (mode) {           // Conflicts with PT_BEGIN's switch
            case 0: /* ... */ break;
            case 1: /* ... */ break;
        }
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 100);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

Fix: Extract the switch into a helper function, or use if/else if:

// ✅ Option A: helper function
static void handle_mode(int mode) {
    switch (mode) {
        case 0: /* ... */ break;
        case 1: /* ... */ break;
    }
}

static SYN_PT_Status my_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        handle_mode(mode);
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 100);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// ✅ Option B: if/else if chain
static SYN_PT_Status my_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        if (mode == 0)      { /* ... */ }
        else if (mode == 1) { /* ... */ }
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 100);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Constraint Workaround Local variables lost across yield/delay Use static, globals, or task->user_data No switch inside task body Extract to a helper function, or use if/else if Task must be a single function Use PT_SPAWN() for subtask decomposition

Return values (SYN_PT_Status):

  • PT_IDLE (0) — nothing to do right now (PT_PASS, false PT_WAIT_UNTIL); scheduler marks the task PASSED for the current round so other ready tasks run first
  • PT_MORE (1) — completed a chunk of work and more work is waiting (PT_CONTINUE); task stays in the scheduler's Work tier
  • PT_EXITED (2) — aborted early via PT_EXIT
  • PT_ENDED (3) — ran to PT_END (normal completion)

docs.title: Scheduler
Priorities & Starvation Windows
docs.text:
SyntropicOS defines four standard priority levels (SYN_Prio in syn_task.h, 0 = highest):

Priority Value Default Max Wait (max_wait_ms) Config Macro Typical Workload SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL 0 1 ms SYN_SCHED_MAX_WAIT_CRITICAL_MS Control loops, safety interlocks, low-latency bus polling SYN_PRIO_HIGH 1 5 ms SYN_SCHED_MAX_WAIT_HIGH_MS Protocol I/O, serial CLI, active frame/event handlers SYN_PRIO_NORMAL 2 15 ms SYN_SCHED_MAX_WAIT_NORMAL_MS Application state machines, UI refresh, periodic sampling SYN_PRIO_LOW 3 50 ms SYN_SCHED_MAX_WAIT_LOW_MS Background batch compute (NN inference, flash GC, logging) 
// Define SYN_USE_* and struct-sizing macros in syn_config.h (or project-wide -D flags)
// so syn_sched.c and application translation units compile with identical layouts:
#define SYN_SCHED_PRIO_LEVELS 4  // default

// Or configure per-instance at runtime (values < 1 clamp to 1 ms):
syn_sched_set_max_wait(&sched, SYN_PRIO_LOW, 25);

docs.title: Cooperative Chunk Sizing Rule
docs.text:
Because protothreads are non-preemptive, the scheduler only regains control at yield points. Keep every uninterrupted execution chunk across all tasks (including SYN_PRIO_LOW) shorter than the tightest active max_wait_ms (1 ms default when SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL is used). Split multi-millisecond loops across PT_CONTINUE(pt) or PT_CONTINUE_IF_NEEDED(pt, task).

Attach a SYN_TaskProfileManager (syntropic/debug/syn_task_profile.h) via syn_sched_set_profiler(&sched, &prof) during development, HIL, or QEMU CI runs and call syn_task_profile_check_budgets(&prof, &sched, &violations, &worst) to verify that no scheduled task's max_yield_us exceeds its participating peers' max_wait_ms budget.

docs.title: Ranked Dispatch & Yield Intent (PT_PASS vs PT_CONTINUE)
docs.text:
On each syn_sched_run() call, eligible (ready, non-delayed, non-blocked) tasks are grouped into ranks. The highest rank with any member wins, and priority followed by round-robin determines the winner inside every rank:

Rank Membership Order Within Rank 1. Overdue (int32_t)(now - due_ms) >= 0 Priority, then round-robin 2. Work MORE set (PT_CONTINUE or woke from sleep/block) Priority, then round-robin 3. Poll Not MORE and not PASSED Priority, then round-robin Round Reset Only PASSED tasks remain Clear all PASSED flags and select by priority, then round-robin

After each dispatch, due_ms = now + max_wait_ms[prio] and the priority level's round-robin cursor advances.

Starvation Bound Guarantee

Every eligible task runs within max_wait_ms[prio] plus the execution time of the cooperative chunk running at that moment plus any higher-priority overdue tasks ahead of it. This is a soft cooperative bound; hard real-time latency belongs in an ISR. If higher priorities consume more than 100% of CPU (sum(run_time / max_wait) > 1), lower priorities shed first by design.

docs.title: Choosing the Right Yield Macro
docs.text: Macro Status Returned Scheduler Effect When to Use PT_PASS(pt) PT_IDLE Marks task PASSED for the current round Polling loops that checked for work and found none, or finished draining PT_CONTINUE(pt) PT_MORE Keeps task in Work rank Chunked processing (e.g. NN layer, HTTP stream, motion step) with remaining backlog PT_CONTINUE_IF_NEEDED(pt, task) PT_MORE (conditional) Yields only if syn_task_should_share(task) is true Drain loops that can process multiple items back-to-back until an equal/higher-priority MORE peer is waiting or any peer reaches its due_ms PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, cond) PT_IDLE (if false) Marks task PASSED for the current round Polled condition waiting (keeps task READY; use PT_BLOCK_* for tickless sleep) PT_BLOCK_EVENT(pt, ...) PT_IDLE + BLOCKED Skipped completely until event flag fires Event-driven tasks and tickless low-power designs

docs.title: Four Standard Task Archetypes
docs.text:
// 1. Periodic task: sleeps until deadline (tickless-compatible, wakes in Work rank)
static SYN_PT_Status blink_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        syn_gpio_toggle(LED_PIN);
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 500);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// 2. Non-blocking poller: PT_CONTINUE while active, PT_PASS when idle
static SYN_PT_Status cli_poll_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    uint8_t byte;
    (void)task;
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        if (uart_try_read_byte(&byte)) {
            syn_cli_process_char(&cli, (char)byte);
            PT_CONTINUE(pt); // More RX bytes likely queued — stay in Work rank
        } else {
            PT_PASS(pt);     // Nothing waiting — pass remainder of round
        }
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// 3. Chunked compute worker: bounded latency per step with PT_CONTINUE
static SYN_PT_Status nn_worker_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    static size_t layer;
    (void)task;
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, inference_requested);
        for (layer = 0; layer < NUM_LAYERS; layer++) {
            run_nn_layer(layer); // Keep each chunk < 1 ms
            PT_CONTINUE(pt);     // More layers remain — share CPU, stay in Work rank
        }
        inference_requested = false;
        PT_PASS(pt);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// 4. Adaptive burst drain: zero yield overhead until a peer actually needs CPU
static SYN_PT_Status rx_drain_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        while (rx_ring_available() > 0) {
            process_one_frame();
            PT_CONTINUE_IF_NEEDED(pt, task); // Yields only on peer contention/due_ms
        }
        PT_PASS(pt); // Queue empty — let lower priorities run this round
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

Anti-Pattern: Unconditional PT_CONTINUE in an Idle Poll Loop

Never end an unconditional poll loop with PT_CONTINUE(pt) when no work was performed: 

// ❌ BAD: stays in Work rank forever even when sensor has no data
for (;;) {
    if (sensor_has_sample()) { read_sample(); }
    PT_CONTINUE(pt); // Forces lower-priority tasks onto their max_wait_ms timer!
}

// ✅ GOOD: only report PT_MORE when work remains; otherwise PT_PASS
for (;;) {
    if (sensor_has_sample()) {
        read_sample();
        PT_CONTINUE(pt);
    } else {
        PT_PASS(pt);
    }
}
Returning PT_MORE when idle defeats Poll rounds (Rank 3) and prevents lower-priority tasks from running until their due_ms starvation deadline expires.

docs.title: True Task Blocking Primitives (SYN_TASK_BLOCKED)
docs.text:
Standard protothread PT_WAIT_UNTIL and PT_WAIT_EVENT use cooperative polling — the task stays SYN_TASK_READY, executes once per polling round, checks its condition, and returns PT_IDLE. While functional, this wastes CPU cycles and prevents tickless sleep hardware low-power modes.

SyntropicOS provides First-Class Native Task Blocking. When a task blocks via PT_BLOCK_EVENT or PT_BLOCK_CONDITION (and its subsystem wrappers), its state transitions to SYN_TASK_BLOCKED and the scheduler skips the task completely on subsequent dispatches (zero CPU polling overhead, tickless-sleep compatible):

#define EVT_DATA_READY  SYN_BIT(0)

static SYN_EventGroup uart_events;

// ISR:
void UART_IRQHandler(void) {
    syn_event_set(&uart_events, EVT_DATA_READY);  // ISR-safe; scheduler auto-wakes blocked waiter
}

// Task:
static SYN_PT_Status uart_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        PT_BLOCK_EVENT(pt, task, &uart_events, EVT_DATA_READY);
        // Wakes here when EVT_DATA_READY is set (flag auto-cleared)
        process_uart_data();
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

docs.title: Native Task Blocking Matrix Across OS Services
docs.text:
Native blocking primitives fall into two distinct wake contracts:

1. Auto-Waking Native Primitives (no manual syn_task_resume(task) required)

Subsystem / Layer Polled Primitive Native Task-Blocking Primitive Automatic Wake Mechanism Event Flags PT_WAIT_EVENT(pt, grp, mask) PT_BLOCK_EVENT(pt, task, grp, mask) / PT_BLOCK_EVENT_WITH_TIMEOUT(pt, task, grp, mask, ms, out) Woken automatically when syn_event_flags_set() / syn_event_set() sets a matching bit (or ms timeout expires) Active Objects — SYN_ActiveObject (syn_ao_init, internal syn_ao_pt_run) Woken automatically by syn_ao_post(ao, sig, data) TCP / UDP Sockets — PT_TCP_BLOCK_READ(...) / PT_UDP_BLOCK_READ(...) Woken automatically by syn_tcp_process_packet(), syn_udp_process_packet(), or syn_udp_unbind()

2. Zero-RAM PT_BLOCK_CONDITION Convenience Wrappers (producer / ISR MUST call syn_task_resume(task))

PT_BLOCK_CONDITION Does Not Poll

PT_BLOCK_CONDITION(pt, task, cond) and the zero-RAM convenience wrappers below do not store a waiter pointer inside the target struct and are not polled by the scheduler. After updating the underlying state, the producer, driver, or ISR must call syn_task_resume(task) so the scheduler re-evaluates cond; omitting syn_task_resume(task) leaves the task parked in SYN_TASK_BLOCKED indefinitely.

Subsystem / Layer Polled Primitive Native Task-Blocking Wrapper Required Producer / ISR Wake Sequence Core Expression PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, cond) PT_BLOCK_CONDITION(pt, task, cond) Update state satisfying cond + syn_task_resume(task) Semaphores PT_SEM_WAIT(pt, sem) PT_SEM_BLOCK(pt, task, sem) PT_SEM_SIGNAL(sem) + syn_task_resume(task) Stream I/O PT_STREAM_WAIT(pt, stream) PT_BLOCK_STREAM(pt, task, stream) syn_stream_put() / syn_stream_write() + syn_task_resume(task) SPSC Queue PT_QUEUE_WAIT_POP(pt, q) PT_BLOCK_QUEUE_POP(pt, task, q) syn_spsc_queue_push() + syn_task_resume(task) DHCP Engine PT_DHCP_WAIT_BOUND(pt, dhcp) PT_DHCP_BLOCK_BOUND(pt, task, dhcp) syn_dhcp_process_packet() state update + syn_task_resume(task) Network Config PT_NETCFG_WAIT_BOUND(pt, netcfg) PT_NETCFG_BLOCK_BOUND(pt, task, netcfg) / PT_NETCFG_BLOCK_LINK_UP(...) syn_netcfg_*() state update + syn_task_resume(task) AutoIP Service PT_AUTOIP_WAIT_BOUND(pt, autoip) PT_AUTOIP_BLOCK_BOUND(pt, task, autoip) syn_autoip_process_arp() state update + syn_task_resume(task) Button Input PT_WAIT_BUTTON_PRESS(pt, btn) / RELEASE PT_BUTTON_BLOCK_PRESS(pt, task, btn) / PT_BUTTON_BLOCK_RELEASE(pt, task, btn) syn_button_update() state update + syn_task_resume(task)
  • Ethernet RX (PT_ETH_WAIT_FRAME): PT_ETH_WAIT_FRAME(pt, rx_buf, max_len, rx_len) is a polled primitive (PT_WAIT_UNTIL over syn_port_eth_rx()). For native task blocking on Ethernet RX, signal an event flag (PT_BLOCK_EVENT) or pair PT_BLOCK_CONDITION with syn_task_resume(task) in the MAC/PHY RX ISR.
  • Mutex Contention (PT_MUTEX_LOCK): PT_MUTEX_LOCK(pt, task, mutex) uses polled PT_WAIT_UNTIL with priority inheritance and promotes the contended waiter into Work rank on syn_mutex_unlock() (keeps contended tasks SYN_TASK_READY and prevents tickless sleep while contended).
Approach Scheduling cost Tickless-safe Use case PT_WAIT_* (Polled) Polled every pass No — prevents sleep Simple standalone / legacy coroutines PT_BLOCK_* (Native) Skipped entirely while blocked Yes Low-power event-driven services

docs.title: Yield-Safe Priority Boosting (syn_task_boost_priority)
docs.text:
Tasks can temporarily elevate their execution priority during critical hardware transactions (e.g. RS-485 frame bursts, SPI flash writes) without risk of stack variable corruption across yields:

static SYN_PT_Status sensor_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 1000);

        // Elevate task to SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL (highest)
        syn_task_boost_priority(task, SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL);

        send_sensor_request();
        PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, sensor_data_ready()); // Yield safe across ticks!
        read_sensor_response();

        // Restore back to configured base priority
        syn_task_restore_priority(task);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}
  • syn_task_boost_priority(task, temp_prio): Monotonic upward priority boost — elevates task->priority to temp_prio only when temp_prio < task->priority (numerically lower SYN_Prio is higher priority; never demotes an already higher manual boost or inherited mutex priority), marks MORE, and tightens due_ms to the boosted priority's wait window.
  • syn_task_restore_priority(task): Restores task->priority to task->base_priority, or retains the highest contended waiter priority across any held SYN_Mutex locks while priority inheritance is active.
  • syn_task_set_base_priority(task, new_prio): Updates task->base_priority permanently and recomputes task->priority while preserving any higher active SYN_Mutex priority inheritance.

docs.title: Priority-Inheriting Mutex (sched/syn_mutex.h)
docs.text:
When tasks at different priorities share a peripheral or multi-step transaction (e.g. shared SPI bus or I2C EEPROM), SYN_Mutex provides recursive cooperative mutual exclusion with automatic priority inheritance:

static SYN_Mutex spi_bus_mtx;

// Initialize once during setup:
syn_mutex_init(&spi_bus_mtx);

// Inside any task (e.g. SYN_PRIO_LOW flash logger or SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL sensor):
static SYN_PT_Status flash_log_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, log_page_full());

        PT_MUTEX_LOCK(pt, task, &spi_bus_mtx);
        spi_select_flash();
        PT_SPAWN(pt, &flash_pt, flash_write_page_pt(&flash_pt));
        spi_deselect_flash();
        PT_MUTEX_UNLOCK(&spi_bus_mtx, task);

        PT_PASS(pt);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}
  • Priority Inheritance: If a higher-priority task calls PT_MUTEX_LOCK while a lower-priority task holds spi_bus_mtx, the holder's priority is immediately boosted to the waiter's priority and promoted into Work rank (MORE set) until PT_MUTEX_UNLOCK releases the outer lock, preventing medium-priority tasks from preempting the holder.
  • Recursive Locking: The owning task may re-acquire the same SYN_Mutex up to UINT16_MAX times; ownership releases when lock_count returns to 0.
  • Non-Blocking Try-Lock: PT_MUTEX_TRYLOCK(&spi_bus_mtx, task) attempts immediate acquisition and returns true on success or false if held by another task.
  • Single-Scheduler (AMP) Scope: All scheduled tasks acquiring or waiting on a SYN_Mutex must belong to the same SYN_Sched instance (SYN_INVALID_PARAM on cross-scheduler contention). For cross-core synchronization in AMP builds, use SYN_SPINLOCK_GUARD() or SPSC syn_mailbox.

docs.title: Task Delay Semantics: "At Least" Minimum Wait Guarantees
docs.text:
In a cooperative operating system like SyntropicOS, all delay macros (PT_TASK_DELAY_MS, PT_DELAY_MS, PT_DELAY_US) guarantee a minimum wait duration ("at least N ms / N us").

Non-Preemptive Delay Guarantee

Delays do not guarantee an exact microsecond or millisecond wakeup time. Because execution is strictly cooperative, a task whose delay has expired will resume on the next scheduler pass after the currently executing task yields. Actual resumption latency equals deadline + execution_time_of_running_tasks.

docs.title: Millisecond vs Microsecond Delays
docs.text:
1. Millisecond Delays (PT_TASK_DELAY_MS):
  2. Managed directly by the scheduler top-level loop (task->delay_until in ms).
  3. Maximum single delay capacity: 24.8 days ($2,147,483,647$ ms).

  4. Ideal for periodic tasks, heartbeat timers, and protocol timeouts.

  5. Microsecond Delays (PT_DELAY_US):

  6. Uses a dedicated, user-supplied persistent target variable (static uint32_t us_target;).
  7. Does not modify task->delay_until, preventing top-level scheduler deadline conflicts.
  8. Evaluated inside the protothread via PT_WAIT_UNTIL against syn_port_get_tick_us(). Returns PT_IDLE while the deadline is pending, allowing other ready tasks to run during the round.
static SYN_PT_Status pulse_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task)
{
    static uint32_t us_target; // Persistent target for microsecond delay

    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        syn_gpio_write(LED_PIN, SYN_GPIO_HIGH);

        // 1. Microsecond delay: minimum 50 µs wait (uses us_target, task->delay_until stays 0)
        PT_DELAY_US(pt, &us_target, 50);

        syn_gpio_write(LED_PIN, SYN_GPIO_LOW);

        // 2. Millisecond delay: minimum 100 ms wait (managed by scheduler in ms)
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 100);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

Task states:

State Value Description SYN_TASK_READY 0 Eligible to run when not delayed SYN_TASK_SUSPENDED 1 Skipped until resumed SYN_TASK_DEAD 2 Exited, will not run again SYN_TASK_BLOCKED 3 Blocked on event/condition — skipped until woken

Task & scheduler control:

  • syn_sched_set_max_wait(sched, prio, ms) — configure per-priority starvation bound (clamped to >= 1 ms)
  • syn_task_should_share(task) — true during task's dispatch if an equal/higher-priority MORE peer is waiting or a peer's due_ms has arrived
  • syn_task_suspend(task) — skip task until resumed
  • syn_task_resume(task) — make task eligible again
  • syn_task_restart(task) — reset protothread and set to READY
  • syn_task_is_alive(task) — check if task is not DEAD
  • syn_sched_alive_count(sched) — count living tasks

docs.title: ISR-Safety Reference
docs.text: Execution Context Functions / Macros ISR-safe syn_task_resume(), syn_event_flags_set() (syn_event_set()), syn_event_flags_clear() (syn_event_clear()), syn_event_flags_get() (syn_event_get()), syn_ao_post(), syn_workqueue_post(), syn_spsc_queue_push() (single-ISR producer), syn_sleep_lock(), syn_sleep_unlock() Task / main-loop context only syn_sched_init(), syn_sched_run*(), syn_sched_set_max_wait(), syn_task_create(), syn_task_suspend(), syn_task_restart(), syn_task_boost_priority(), syn_task_restore_priority(), syn_task_set_base_priority(), syn_mutex_try_lock(), syn_mutex_unlock()

docs.title: Timers & Scheduling Extensions
docs.text: Module Header Config Description Timers sched/syn_timer.h SYN_USE_TIMER Software timers — one-shot and periodic callbacks driven by syn_port_get_tick_ms() Timer Wheel sched/syn_timer_wheel.h Always available O(1) 64-bucket hashed timing wheel (syn_timer_wheel_add, syn_timer_wheel_cancel, syn_timer_wheel_step) for high-count one-shot timeouts Events sched/syn_event_flags.h / util/syn_event.h SYN_USE_EVENT 32-bit atomic event flag groups (SYN_EventFlags / SYN_EventGroup) for ISR & inter-task signaling Watchdog sched/syn_watchdog.h SYN_USE_WATCHDOG Per-task software check-in deadlines. Timeout events auto-record to syn_errlog if configured. Sequencer sched/syn_sequencer.h SYN_USE_SEQUENCER Step-based async sequence runner for timed action chains Work Queue sched/syn_workqueue.h SYN_USE_WORKQUEUE Deferred work queue — safely post work from ISR to main thread Mailbox sched/syn_mailbox.h Always available Typed single-producer/single-consumer (SPSC) message queue (header-only) Active Object sched/syn_ao.h SYN_USE_AO Active Object execution context — combines FSM + SYN_Mailbox + caller-owned scheduler task

docs.title: Tickless Idle
docs.text:
Module Header Config Tickless Idle sched/syn_sched.h SYN_USE_TICKLESS — Low-power sleep between task deadlines (requires: SCHED)

Enabled via SYN_USE_TICKLESS 1 in syn_config.h. Off by default — the scheduler is unchanged unless you opt in.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
In a normal syn_sched_run_forever() loop, the CPU busy-loops when no tasks are ready. Tickless idle replaces that with low-power sleep (syn_sched_run_tickless() for task deadlines, or syn_sched_run_tickless_ex() when SYN_Timer deadlines must also wake the CPU):

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                syn_sched_run_tickless()                │
│                                                        │
│  +---> Run all ready tasks (syn_sched_run)             │
│  |                                                     │
│  |    Any tasks ready NOW?                             │
│  |    |- Yes -> loop back, run them                    │
│  |    \- No  -> compute next wakeup deadline           │
│  |             |                                       │
│  |             |- Deadline exists -> sleep until it    │
│  |             |   syn_port_sleep_until(wake_tick)     │
│  |             |                                       │
│  |             \- No deadlines  -> light sleep         │
│  |                 syn_sleep_enter(sleep)              │
│  |                                                     │
│  |    <--- CPU wakes (timer alarm OR interrupt) --->   │
│  +───────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Interrupts and Wakeup
docs.text:
The key insight: syn_port_sleep_until() returns on any interrupt, not just the timer alarm. This is how interrupts integrate naturally:

Wakeup Source What Happens Timer alarm fires CPU wakes at the scheduled tick. The scheduler runs delayed tasks that are now due. EXTI / GPIO interrupt CPU wakes early. The ISR runs (e.g., button press, sensor data-ready). If the ISR posts work via syn_workqueue_post() or sets an event via syn_event_set(), the scheduler picks it up on the next loop iteration. UART / SPI / DMA interrupt Same — ISR runs, fills a ring buffer/stream or signals a semaphore, and calls syn_task_resume(task) (or syn_event_set()). The scheduler runs the woken task. Any other IRQ CPU wakes, ISR runs, scheduler re-evaluates. If nothing is ready, it goes back to sleep.

The scheduler doesn't need to know about your interrupts. It simply re-checks task readiness every time it wakes up. The idle loop is:

  1. Run ready tasks
  2. No tasks ready? → Sleep until the next deadline (or forever)
  3. Wake up (timer or interrupt) → goto 1

Polling Tasks Prevent Tickless Sleep

syn_sched_next_wakeup() returns now whenever any SYN_TASK_READY task has delay_until == 0 — including any task yielded via PT_PASS(pt) or polling on PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, cond) / PT_DELAY_US(...). Whenever wake == now, sleep entry is skipped immediately. In a tickless system, every task must park in PT_TASK_DELAY_MS, PT_BLOCK_* (SYN_TASK_BLOCKED), SYN_TASK_SUSPENDED, or SYN_TASK_DEAD when idle.

docs.title: Wakelocks & Sleep Control
docs.text:
If a peripheral needs the CPU to stay awake (e.g., mid-UART or DMA transfer), acquire a named lock bit on the SYN_Sleep coordinator:

#define LOCK_UART_TX SYN_SLEEP_LOCK_UART

syn_sleep_lock(&sleep, LOCK_UART_TX);    // Prevent sleep (ISR-safe)
// ... do time-critical work ...
syn_sleep_unlock(&sleep, LOCK_UART_TX);  // Allow sleep again

While any wakelock bit is held, when syn_sleep_enable(&sleep, false) has disabled sleep globally, or when sleep is configured with SYN_SLEEP_NONE, syn_sched_run_tickless() and syn_sched_run_tickless_ex() skip hardware sleep and busy-loop like syn_sched_run_forever().

docs.title: Example: Button + Periodic Task
docs.text:
// syn_config.h (must be visible when compiling syn_sched.c as well as app TUs)
#define SYN_USE_TICKLESS 1

static SYN_Task tasks[2];
static SYN_Sched sched;
static SYN_Sleep sleep;

// Task A: blink LED every 1 second
static SYN_PT_Status blink_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task) {
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        syn_gpio_toggle(LED_PIN);
        PT_TASK_DELAY_MS(pt, task, 1000);
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

// Task B: respond to button press (EXTI sets event flag and wakes CPU)
static SYN_PT_Status button_task(SYN_PT *pt, SYN_Task *task) {
    PT_BEGIN(pt);
    for (;;) {
        PT_BLOCK_EVENT(pt, task, &btn_events, EVT_BUTTON_PRESSED);
        handle_button();
    }
    PT_END(pt);
}

int main(void) {
    syn_event_init(&btn_events);
    syn_task_create(&tasks[0], "blink",  blink_task,  SYN_PRIO_NORMAL,   NULL);
    syn_task_create(&tasks[1], "button", button_task, SYN_PRIO_CRITICAL, NULL);
    syn_sched_init(&sched, tasks, 2);
    syn_sleep_init(&sleep, SYN_SLEEP_DEEP);

    // CPU sleeps between 1-second blinks.
    // Button EXTI wakes it early when pressed.
    syn_sched_run_tickless(&sched, &sleep);
}

Between blinks, blink_task is delayed and button_task is SYN_TASK_BLOCKED, so the CPU enters low-power mode for ~1 second. If a button EXTI fires at 500 ms, the CPU wakes immediately, the ISR calls syn_event_set(&btn_events, EVT_BUTTON_PRESSED), and the scheduler runs button_task before returning to sleep for the remaining ~500 ms until the next blink.

docs.title: Port Requirement
docs.text:
Implement syn_port_sleep_until(uint32_t wake_tick_ms) in your platform port. This function must:

  1. Program a hardware wake timer (RTC alarm, LPTIM compare, etc.) for wake_tick_ms
  2. Enter a low-power mode (e.g., __WFI() on Cortex-M)
  3. Return when the alarm fires or any interrupt wakes the CPU

The default weak stub falls back to syn_port_sleep(SYN_SLEEP_LIGHT) (no timer programming — just WFI).

docs.title: Timer-Aware Tickless (run_tickless_ex)
docs.text:
When using software timers alongside tickless idle, the basic syn_sched_run_tickless() only considers task delay_until deadlines. Software timer expirations won't wake the CPU — they'll fire late, after the next task wakes up.

syn_sched_run_tickless_ex() solves this by combining both:

                             syn_sched_run_tickless_ex()
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. Run scheduler (syn_sched_run)                          │
│  2. Service software timers (syn_timer_service)            │
│  3. sleep_until = min(next_task_wakeup, next_timer_expiry) │
│  4. Enter low-power sleep until sleep_until                │
│  5. goto 1                                                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Requires both SYN_USE_TICKLESS and SYN_USE_TIMER to be enabled.

// syn_config.h
#define SYN_USE_TICKLESS 1
#define SYN_USE_TIMER    1

static SYN_Timer timers[2];
syn_timer_init(&timers[0], 100, true, sensor_poll_cb, NULL);
syn_timer_init(&timers[1], 5000, true, heartbeat_cb, NULL);
syn_timer_start(&timers[0]);
syn_timer_start(&timers[1]);

// CPU wakes for both task delays AND timer expirations
syn_sched_run_tickless_ex(&sched, &sleep, timers, 2);

syn_timer_next_expiry() is also available standalone if you need to query the earliest timer deadline:

uint32_t next = syn_timer_next_expiry(timers, timer_count);
// UINT32_MAX if no active timers

docs.title: Multicore (AMP)
docs.text:
Enable SYN_USE_MULTICORE to add Asymmetric Multiprocessing support. Each core runs its own independent cooperative scheduler; cores communicate via the existing mailbox (upgraded with memory barriers) and protect shared peripherals with spinlocks.

Key files:

File Purpose syn_barrier.h Acquire/release memory ordering primitives syn_port_spinlock.h Spinlock, core ID, and IPC notify port functions syn_spinlock.h Scoped SYN_SPINLOCK_GUARD() helper syn_mailbox.h SPSC mailbox (barrier-upgraded for cross-core safety)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Core 0                         Core 1
   ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐
   │ SYN_Sched sched0 │          │ SYN_Sched sched1 │
   │ tasks0[N]        │          │ tasks1[M]        │
   │                  │          │                  │
   │ run_forever()    │<-------->│ run_forever()    │
   │                  │ Mailbox  │                  │
   └──────────────────┘          └──────────────────┘

Each core owns its own scheduler, task array, and timers. No changes to the cooperative protothread model. Cross-core coordination uses only two primitives: - Mailbox — typed message passing (SPSC, lock-free) - Spinlock — mutual exclusion for shared hardware (UART, flash, etc.)

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
// syn_config.h
#define SYN_USE_MULTICORE   1
#define SYN_SPINLOCK_COUNT  4  // number of spinlock IDs (default 4)

docs.title: Cross-Core Mailbox
docs.text:
The existing syn_mailbox is automatically upgraded with acquire/release barriers when SYN_USE_MULTICORE=1. On single-core builds, these compile to zero-cost plain volatile access.

typedef struct { uint8_t id; int32_t value; } SensorMsg;

// Place in shared SRAM accessible to both cores
SYN_MAILBOX_DEFINE(ipc_mbox, SensorMsg, 16);

// Optional: wake consumer core on post
syn_mailbox_set_notify(&ipc_mbox, true);

// Core 0 (producer):
SensorMsg msg = { .id = 1, .value = 42 };
syn_mailbox_post(&ipc_mbox, &msg);

// Core 1 (consumer):
SensorMsg rx;
if (syn_mailbox_receive(&ipc_mbox, &rx)) {
    handle(rx.id, rx.value);
}

Warning: The mailbox is strictly single-producer, single-consumer. If you need multiple producers, serialize access with a spinlock.

docs.title: Spinlocks
docs.text:
Spinlocks protect shared resources (peripherals, log buffers) across cores. They disable interrupts on the acquiring core to prevent priority inversion.

#include "syntropic/util/syn_spinlock.h"

// Scoped lock — guaranteed release on scope exit
SYN_SPINLOCK_GUARD(SYN_SPINLOCK_UART) {
    syn_port_uart_transmit(0, data, len, 10);
}

// Manual lock (for more control)
syn_port_spinlock_acquire(SYN_SPINLOCK_FLASH);
syn_port_flash_write(addr, buf, len);
syn_port_spinlock_release(SYN_SPINLOCK_FLASH);

Well-known lock IDs:

ID Macro Purpose 0 SYN_SPINLOCK_UART Shared UART 1 SYN_SPINLOCK_FLASH Shared flash 2 SYN_SPINLOCK_USER0 Application use 3 SYN_SPINLOCK_USER1 Application use

docs.title: Porting Guide
docs.text:
Implement these functions for your platform:

// Required:
void     syn_port_spinlock_acquire(uint8_t id);   // disable IRQ + spin
void     syn_port_spinlock_release(uint8_t id);   // release + restore IRQ
bool     syn_port_spinlock_try_acquire(uint8_t id);
uint8_t  syn_port_core_id(void);                  // return 0 or 1
void     syn_port_memory_barrier(void);           // DMB on ARM, __sync_synchronize fallback

// Optional (no-op stub provided):
void     syn_port_ipc_notify(void);               // SEV on ARM, triggers WFE wakeup

RP2040 example — hardware spinlocks:

#include "hardware/sync.h"

static spin_lock_t *locks[SYN_SPINLOCK_COUNT];
static uint32_t saved_irq[SYN_SPINLOCK_COUNT];

void syn_port_spinlock_acquire(uint8_t id) {
    saved_irq[id] = spin_lock_blocking(locks[id]);
}

void syn_port_spinlock_release(uint8_t id) {
    spin_unlock(locks[id], saved_irq[id]);
}

void syn_port_memory_barrier(void) {
    __dmb();  // Data Memory Barrier
}

void syn_port_ipc_notify(void) {
    __sev();  // Send Event — wakes other core from WFE
}

docs.title: System Services & Utility Modules
docs.text: SyntropicOS provides high-level system services for interactive command line interfaces, software watchdog monitoring, logging, and time synchronization.

docs.title: 1. Interactive Serial CLI (cli/syn_cli.h)
docs.text: The syn_cli module enables zero-allocation, interactive command-line interfaces over UART or USB Virtual COM Port.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Command registry with argument parsing (argc, argv).
  • Built-in help command automatically listing all registered commands and descriptions.
  • Backspace, Line-feed (\r\n), and prompt string management ("> ").

docs.title: Complete Code Example
docs.text:
#include <syntropic/cli/syn_cli.h>
#include <syntropic/port/syn_port_serial.h>

static SYN_CLI cli;

// Command 1: Echo handler
static int cmd_echo(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    if (argc < 2) {
        syn_cli_printf(&cli, "Usage: echo <text>\r\n");
        return 1;
    }
    syn_cli_printf(&cli, "Echo: %s\r\n", argv[1]);
    return 0;
}

// Command 2: System info handler
static int cmd_info(int argc, char *argv[]) {
    (void)argc; (void)argv;
    syn_cli_printf(&cli, "SyntropicOS v1.0.0\r\nUptime: %lu ms\r\n",
                   (unsigned long)syn_port_get_tick_ms());
    return 0;
}

static const SYN_CLI_Command command_table[] = {
    { "echo", "Echo argument back to terminal", cmd_echo },
    { "info", "Print system version and uptime", cmd_info },
};

void app_init(void) {
    syn_port_serial_init(115200);

    // Initialize CLI with command table and prompt
    syn_cli_init(&cli, command_table, sizeof(command_table)/sizeof(command_table[0]), "> ");
    syn_cli_printf(&cli, "\r\n--- SyntropicOS Serial CLI ---\r\n");
    syn_cli_print_prompt(&cli);
}

void app_loop(void) {
    uint8_t rx_char;
    if (syn_port_serial_read(&rx_char, 1) > 0) {
        // Feed character into CLI state machine
        syn_cli_process_char(&cli, (char)rx_char);
    }
}

docs.title: 2. Multi-Task Software Watchdog (sched/syn_watchdog.h)
docs.text:
The software watchdog monitors per-task check-in deadlines and invokes a timeout callback (typically syn_port_system_reset()) if any registered task misses its window.

#include <stdio.h>
#include <syntropic/port/syn_port_system.h>
#include <syntropic/sched/syn_watchdog.h>

static SYN_Watchdog wdt;
static SYN_WDT_Entry entries[3];
static int8_t sensor_wdt_id;

static void on_wdt_timeout(SYN_Watchdog *w, const SYN_WDT_Entry *entry, void *ctx) {
    (void)w;
    (void)ctx;
    printf("ERROR: Task '%s' missed %lu ms deadline! Resetting system...\n",
           entry->name, (unsigned long)entry->timeout_ms);
    syn_port_system_reset();
}

void task_worker(void) {
    // Reset check-in deadline for registered task
    syn_watchdog_checkin(&wdt, sensor_wdt_id);
}

void app_init(void) {
    // Initialize watchdog with 3 caller-owned entry slots and timeout callback
    syn_watchdog_init(&wdt, entries, 3, on_wdt_timeout, NULL);
    sensor_wdt_id = syn_watchdog_register(&wdt, "sensor", 2000);
}

void app_check_watchdog(void) {
    // Evaluate all active task deadlines
    syn_watchdog_update(&wdt);
}

docs.title: 3. Structured Logging, Binary Data Logger & Flight Blackbox (log/*.h)
docs.text:
• Structured Console & Custom-Sink Logger (log/syn_log.h, SYN_USE_LOG):
  • Tagged, severity-filtered logging (SYN_LOG_T, SYN_LOG_D, SYN_LOG_I, SYN_LOG_W, SYN_LOG_E, SYN_LOG_F) plus syn_log_raw() and syn_log_hexdump().
  • Calls below compile-time SYN_LOG_LEVEL (0 = TRACE .. 5 = FATAL, 6 = NONE) compile out to ((void)0).
  • syn_log_init(NULL, SYN_LOG_INFO) routes output to syn_port_serial_write(); pass a SYN_LogOutputFn callback (syn_log_init(my_sink_fn, SYN_LOG_INFO)) for RTT, SWO/ITM, USB CDC, or file backends.
  • Framed Ring-Buffer Data Logger (log/syn_datalog.h, SYN_USE_DATALOG):
  • Records binary telemetry packets prefixed with SYN_DataLogHeader (uint16_t id, uint16_t len) into a caller-owned SYN_RingBuf (syn_datalog_init, syn_datalog_write, syn_datalog_read) with dropped-frame accounting (syn_datalog_get_dropped).
  • High-Rate Flight Telemetry Blackbox (log/syn_blackbox.h, SYN_USE_BLACKBOX):
  • Compresses SYN_Blackbox_Record frames (3-axis gyro/accel, 4 setpoints, 4 motor outputs, microsecond timestamp) into full Intra ('I', syn_blackbox_encode_intra_ex) and ZigZag-LEB128 delta Predictive ('P', syn_blackbox_encode_delta_ex) frames for flash or SD storage.

docs.title: Storage & Non-Volatile Memory Modules
docs.text: SyntropicOS provides persistent storage components scaling from wear-leveled flash parameters to virtual filesystem abstractions supporting LittleFS and FAT.

docs.title: 1. Persistent Settings Manager (syn_settings.h)
docs.text: The syn_settings module simplifies non-volatile configuration management. It wraps syn_param to provide: - Load-or-Default Initialization: Loads saved configuration from flash on startup, automatically applying factory default values if flash is uninitialized or corrupted. - CRC-16 Checksum Validation: Automatically tracks data integrity and detects changes. - Wear-Leveling Protection: Prevents unnecessary flash erase cycles by only writing when data actually changes. - Change Callbacks: Triggers application callbacks when settings are updated.

docs.title: Storage Pipeline Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Init["syn_settings_init"] --> CheckFlash{"Valid CRC in Flash?"}
    CheckFlash -->|Yes| LoadFlash["Load Settings from Flash"]
    CheckFlash -->|No / Corrupted| ApplyDefault["Apply Factory Defaults & Save"]
    LoadFlash --> AppReady["Application Ready"]
    ApplyDefault --> AppReady
    AppReady -->|Modify Data & Save| CheckDirty{"Data Changed?"}
    CheckDirty -->|Yes| WriteFlash["Compute CRC-16 & Write Flash"]
    CheckDirty -->|No| SkipWrite["Skip Write (Protect Flash Wear)"]

docs.title: Complete Code Example
docs.text:
#include <syntropic/storage/syn_settings.h>

// Define custom application configuration struct
typedef struct {
    uint32_t baud_rate;
    uint16_t node_id;
    uint8_t  display_brightness;
} SystemConfig;

// Factory default values
static const SystemConfig default_config = {
    .baud_rate = 115200,
    .node_id = 0x01,
    .display_brightness = 80
};

static SystemConfig active_config;
static SYN_Settings settings_store;

void on_config_changed(SYN_Settings *store, void *ctx) {
    printf("Config updated! New Node ID: 0x%02X\n", active_config.node_id);
}

void app_init(void) {
    // Flash sector base address = 0x080E0000, Sector Copies = 2 (ping-pong wear leveling)
    syn_settings_init(&settings_store, 0x080E0000, 2,
                      &active_config, sizeof(active_config), &default_config);

    // Register callback for when settings change
    syn_settings_on_change(&settings_store, on_config_changed, NULL);

    printf("Active Baud Rate: %lu\n", (unsigned long)active_config.baud_rate);
}

void update_node_id(uint16_t new_id) {
    active_config.node_id = new_id;

    // Computes CRC-16 and writes flash ONLY if node_id actually changed
    syn_settings_save(&settings_store);
}

docs.title: 2. Flash Wear-Leveling Engine (syn_param.h)
docs.text: The syn_param module provides low-overhead, power-fail-safe, wear-leveled storage directly on raw Flash sectors or pages without requiring a filesystem.

docs.title: Architecture & Memory Layout
docs.text:
Flash is divided into $K$ contiguous sectors or pages. Each sector is partitioned into fixed-size slots aligned to 16-byte boundaries:

flowchart LR
    subgraph S0["Sector 0 (Active)"]
        s0_0["Slot 0<br/>(Seq 1)"]
        s0_1["Slot 1<br/>(Seq 2)"]
        s0_2["Slot 2<br/>(Seq 3 - Active)"]
        s0_3["Slot 3<br/>(0xFF Blank)"]
    end
    subgraph S1["Sector 1 (Standby)"]
        s1_0["Slot 0<br/>(0xFF Blank)"]
        s1_1["Slot 1<br/>(0xFF Blank)"]
        s1_2["Slot 2<br/>(0xFF Blank)"]
        s1_3["Slot 3<br/>(0xFF Blank)"]
    end
    s0_2 -->|Next Save| s0_3
    s0_3 -->|Sector Full -> Erase & Rotate| s1_0

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
1. Sequential Append Writes:
  2. Updates are written to the next blank slot in the current sector (active_slot++) without erasing flash.

  3. Flash write alignment is enforced via align16(sizeof(SYN_ParamSlotHeader) + data_size) to satisfy MCU flash programming parallelism constraints.

  4. Circular Sector Rotation & Erase Minimization:

  5. When all slots in active_sector are exhausted (active_slot >= slots_per_sector), the store rotates to the next sector: $$\text{active_sector} = (\text{active_sector} + 1) \pmod{\text{sector_count}}$$
  6. Only the incoming sector is erased (syn_port_flash_erase).

  7. Total write cycles before any single flash sector reaches its physical erase endurance limit ($E$): $$\text{Total Lifetime Writes} = E \times \text{sector_count} \times \left\lfloor \frac{\text{sector_size}}{\text{slot_size}} \right\rfloor$$ Example: 2 sectors of 4 KB storing a 16-byte payload ($\text{slot_size} = 32\text{ bytes}$) yields $128 \text{ slots/sector} \times 2 \times 10,000 \text{ cycles} = \mathbf{2,560,000\text{ write cycles}}$.

  8. Two-Phase Atomic Commit Protocol:

  9. Phase 1 (Payload Write): The parameter payload is written to flash at slot_addr + sizeof(SYN_ParamSlotHeader).
  10. Phase 2 (Header Commit): The 16-byte header containing SYN_PARAM_MAGIC (0xC0DE) and the CRC-16 checksum is written last.

  11. If power is cut during Phase 1, the slot lacks the 0xC0DE magic signature or fails CRC validation on boot, causing the engine to cleanly ignore the partial write and retain the previous valid slot.

  12. Boot Recovery & Sequence Integer Rollover:

  13. On boot, syn_param_init() scans all slots across all configured sectors.
  14. Sequence comparisons use signed 16-bit modular arithmetic: $$\text{is_newer} = ((\text{int16_t})(\text{hdr.seq} - \text{best_seq}) > 0)$$

  15. This handles 16-bit sequence number rollover ($65535 \rightarrow 0$) without data loss.

  16. Power-Loss Fault Recovery Matrix:

Fault Scenario State of Old Data State of New Data Recovery on Reboot (syn_param_init) Power-loss during Erase Intact in previous sector Partial erase (corrupted bits) Discards erased sector; recovers latest valid slot from previous sector. Re-erases on next write. Power-loss during Data Write Intact in previous slot Partial payload Header missing (0xFF != 0xC0DE); discards incomplete slot and loads previous valid slot. Power-loss during Header Write Intact in previous slot Corrupted header Magic / CRC-16 check fails; discards corrupt slot and loads previous valid slot.

docs.title: 3. Virtual File System (syn_vfs.h)
docs.text: SyntropicOS provides a unified Virtual File System (VFS) interface to abstract raw storage media (Internal Flash, SPI NOR Flash, SD Cards).

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Standardized POSIX-like API (syn_vfs_open, syn_vfs_read, syn_vfs_write, syn_vfs_close).
  • Mount points for LittleFS (syn_lfs) and FAT (syn_fat).

docs.title: Supported Filesystems
docs.text: Module Header Ideal Use Case LittleFS storage/syn_lfs.h NOR Flash memory, power-fail safe, wear-leveled FAT / FAT32 storage/syn_fat.h SD Cards, USB Mass Storage, PC-readable drives Param Store storage/syn_param.h Sector-based raw parameter storage without a filesystem

docs.title: System Architecture & Recovery Modules
docs.text: SyntropicOS provides production-grade system resilience services, including crash-loop boot management, fault-recording core dumps, transport-agnostic OTA firmware updates, and persistent error registries.

docs.title: Architecture Resilience Map
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    PowerOn["System Power On"] --> BootMgr["Boot Manager (syn_boot)"]
    BootMgr -->|Crash Count Exceeded| SafeMode["Safe Mode Boot / Fallback Slot"]
    BootMgr -->|Normal Boot| CheckDump{"Previous HardFault Core Dump?"}
    CheckDump -->|Yes| SaveErrLog["Record Crash Registers to syn_errlog"]
    CheckDump -->|No| AppInit["Initialize System & Tasks"]
    SaveErrLog --> AppInit
    AppInit --> RunLoop["Scheduler Task Loop"]
    RunLoop -->|HardFault / Crash| CoreDumpSave["syn_coredump_save to Flash Sector"]
    CoreDumpSave --> Reset["System Reset"]

docs.title: 1. Boot Manager & Safe-Mode (system/syn_boot.h)
docs.text: The syn_boot module tracks continuous boot cycles and consecutive unconfirmed boots across resets. If the system resets repeatedly without marking a boot healthy, the boot manager enters Safe Mode to allow firmware recovery.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Configurable consecutive failed-boot threshold (safe_threshold) persisted via SYN_ParamStore.
  • Optional boot event recording to syn_errlog (syn_boot_set_errlog(), syn_boot_log_events()).
  • Safe mode fallback flag query (syn_boot_is_safe_mode()).

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
#include <syntropic/system/syn_boot.h>

static SYN_Boot boot;
static SYN_ParamStore boot_store;

void app_boot_check(void) {
    // Persist boot state across 2 flash sectors at 0x08030000; enter safe mode after 3 failures
    syn_param_init(&boot_store, 0x08030000, 2, sizeof(SYN_BootData));
    syn_boot_init(&boot, &boot_store, 3);

    if (syn_boot_is_safe_mode(&boot)) {
        printf("WARNING: Crash loop detected! Booting into SAFE MODE...\n");
        // Start minimal recovery task (e.g., Serial CLI or OTA UART update)
    } else {
        printf("Normal boot sequence proceeding.\n");
    }
}

void app_main_ready(void) {
    // Call once system initialization completes to reset fail_count
    syn_boot_mark_healthy(&boot);
}

docs.title: 2. Core Dump & Hardware Fault Recovery (system/syn_coredump.h & system/syn_fault.h)
docs.text: When a hardware fault (e.g. ARM Cortex-M HardFault, BusFault, or Memory Management Fault) occurs, syn_coredump captures the CPU registers (PC, LR, SP, PSR) and a stack snapshot, persisting them to flash before resetting.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Zero-heap register and stack capture inside fault ISR handler.
  • Reads back register snapshot on next boot for post-mortem diagnostics.

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
#include <syntropic/system/syn_coredump.h>
#include <syntropic/system/syn_fault.h>

void check_previous_crash(void) {
    SYN_CoreDump dump;

    // Read and verify previous crash dump from flash
    if (syn_coredump_read(&dump)) {
        printf("CRASH DETECTED on last boot!\n");
        printf("  Fault PC:  0x%08X\n", (unsigned int)dump.regs.pc);
        printf("  Fault LR:  0x%08X\n", (unsigned int)dump.regs.lr);
        printf("  Uptime:    %lu ms\n", (unsigned long)dump.uptime_ms);

        // Clear core dump after reading
        syn_coredump_clear();
    }
}

// Called from Cortex-M HardFault_Handler assembly stub with stacked exception frame pointer
void hardfault_capture_frame(const uint32_t *sp) {
    SYN_FaultContext ctx = {
        .r0 = sp[0],
        .r1 = sp[1],
        .r2 = sp[2],
        .r3 = sp[3],
        .r12 = sp[4],
        .lr = sp[5],
        .pc = sp[6],
        .xpsr = sp[7],
        .sp = (uint32_t)(uintptr_t)sp,
    };
    syn_fault_capture(&ctx);
    syn_coredump_save(&ctx);

    syn_port_system_reset();
}

docs.title: 3. Persistent Error Log (system/syn_errlog.h)
docs.text:
The syn_errlog module maintains a circular error registry storing application error code, severity, boot count, timestamp, and context value.

#include <syntropic/system/syn_errlog.h>

#define ERR_TIMEOUT 0x1001U

static SYN_ErrLog errlog;
static SYN_ErrEntry log_buffer[16];

void app_setup_errlog(uint32_t current_boot_count) {
    syn_errlog_init(&errlog, log_buffer, 16, current_boot_count);

    // Log an error event
    syn_errlog_record(&errlog, ERR_TIMEOUT, SYN_ERR_ERROR, 0x0042);
}

docs.title: 4. Transport-Agnostic Firmware Update (system/syn_fwupdate.h)
docs.text:
Provides streaming, block-by-block OTA firmware image flashing with running CRC-32 verification and optional HMAC-SHA256, Ed25519, or AES-GCM authentication.

#include <syntropic/system/syn_fwupdate.h>

#define SLOT_B_ADDR 0x08040000U
#define SLOT_B_SIZE 0x00020000U

static uint8_t page_buf[256];
static SYN_FwUpdate fw;

void ota_start(void) {
    syn_fwupdate_begin(&fw, SLOT_B_ADDR, SLOT_B_SIZE, page_buf, sizeof(page_buf));
}

void on_ota_chunk_received(const uint8_t *chunk, size_t len) {
    // Stream incoming firmware chunks over UART, Wi-Fi, BLE, or CAN
    syn_fwupdate_write(&fw, chunk, len);
}

SYN_Status ota_complete(uint32_t expected_crc, uint32_t new_version) {
    return syn_fwupdate_finish(&fw, expected_crc, new_version);
}

docs.title: 5. Dual-Bank A/B Bootloader & Streaming OTA Orchestrator (syn_fwimage.h, syn_fwboot.h, syn_ota.h)
docs.text:
• Firmware Slot Image Header (system/syn_fwimage.h, SYN_USE_BOOT): Defines SYN_FwImageHeader (SYN_FW_MAGIC = 0x53594E46u), slot lifecycle states (EMPTY, WRITING, NEW, TESTING, CONFIRMED, INVALID), CRC-32 header sealing (syn_fwimage_seal_header), and Ed25519 / HMAC image signature checks (syn_fwimage_verify_signature).
  • Dual-Bank A/B Slot Selector (system/syn_fwboot.h, SYN_USE_BOOT): SYN_FwBootManager (syn_fwboot_init, syn_fwboot_select, syn_fwboot_confirm, syn_fwboot_vector_addr) selects the active slot across resets and automatically rolls back unconfirmed TESTING images on crash reboot.
  • Secure Streaming OTA Manager (system/syn_ota.h, SYN_USE_OTA): SYN_OTA_Manager coordinates chunked downloads over HTTP, CoAP, BLE, LwM2M, or UART directly into the inactive A/B flash slot (syn_ota_init, syn_ota_set_verification_key, syn_ota_begin, syn_ota_write_chunk, syn_ota_finish, syn_ota_apply) supporting CRC-32, HMAC-SHA256, Ed25519, and AES-GCM modes.

docs.title: 6. Power Monitor, Sleep Coordinator, Hardware Watchdog & Build Metadata
docs.text:
• Supply Voltage & Brownout Monitor (system/syn_power.h, SYN_USE_POWER): SYN_Power (syn_power_init, syn_power_update, syn_power_voltage_mv) pairs an ADC channel with SYN_Hysteresis thresholds (brownout_mv / restore_mv), brownout/restore callbacks, and optional SYN_ErrLog / SYN_Signal recording.
  • Low-Power Sleep Coordinator (system/syn_sleep.h, always available): SYN_Sleep (syn_sleep_init, syn_sleep_lock, syn_sleep_unlock, syn_sleep_enter) tracks peripheral wake-lock bitmasks (SYN_SLEEP_LOCK_UART, SPI, I2C, DMA, ADC, APP0..3) and coordinates SYN_SLEEP_LIGHT / SYN_SLEEP_DEEP entry with the tickless scheduler.
  • Hardware Watchdog Driver (system/syn_hwwdt.h, SYN_USE_HWWDT): Thin wrapper (syn_hwwdt_init(timeout_ms), syn_hwwdt_feed()) over syn_port_wdt.h for independent MCU watchdog timer reload.
  • Compile-Time Version Metadata (system/syn_version.h, header-only): Exposes CalVer constants (SYN_VERSION_YEAR, SYN_VERSION_MONTH, SYN_VERSION_RELEASE, SYN_VERSION_CODE) and syn_version() returning static SYN_Version build/git metadata.

docs.title: WebAssembly (WASM) Virtual Machine Module
docs.text: The syn_wasm module provides a 100% zero-heap, non-blocking 32-bit WebAssembly MVP cooperative interpreter designed for embedded microcontrollers. It supports static linear memory arrays, zero-copy module loading from Flash memory, host function registration, and instruction-sliced execution with protothread (syn_pt) scheduling.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Zero-Heap Execution: All stack frames, local variables, and global states are allocated inside static structures.
  • Embedded C Compiler Compatibility: Designed for standard C code compiled via clang --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown.
  • Customizable RAM Footprint: Linear memory size and stack depth are user-configurable down to microcontrollers with <4KB RAM.
  • Host Function Integration: Register C native callback functions to expose OS APIs (syn_log, syn_gpio, timers) to WASM programs.
  • Protothread Cooperative Slicing: Execute WASM instructions in time-sliced increments (syn_wasm_step) without blocking system responsiveness.
  • Fixed-Point Math Option: Optional SYN_WASM_USE_FIXED=1 mode maps f32/f64 operations to syn_qmath.h Q16.16 fixed-point arithmetic on FPU-less microcontrollers.

docs.title: Recommended C-to-WASM Compilation Command
docs.text:
To compile standard C applications into WASM binaries compatible with syn_wasm, use LLVM Clang:

clang --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown -O2 -nostdlib \
  -mbulk-memory -msign-ext -mmultivalue -mnontrapping-fptoint \
  -Wl,--no-entry -Wl,--export-all -Wl,--allow-undefined \
  -Wl,-z,stack-size=1024 app.c -o app.wasm

docs.title: Compiler Flags Summary
docs.text: Flag Purpose --target=wasm32-unknown-unknown Targets 32-bit WebAssembly architecture -O2 -nostdlib Optimization level 2 with zero C standard library bloat -mbulk-memory Enables WASM 0xFC bulk memory instructions (memory.copy, memory.fill) -msign-ext Enables sign extension instructions -mnontrapping-fptoint Enables non-trapping saturating float-to-int conversions -Wl,--no-entry Omits standard _start entry point requirement -Wl,--export-all Exports all declared C functions for lookup via syn_wasm_find_export -Wl,--allow-undefined Permits extern host function declarations -Wl,-z,stack-size=1024 Limits internal WASM stack memory to 1KB for embedded RAM compatibility

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
Configure VM parameters in syn_config.h or via compiler build flags:

#define SYN_WASM_MAX_STACK       64    /* Evaluation stack depth */
#define SYN_WASM_MAX_LOCALS     256    /* Total local variables across all frames */
#define SYN_WASM_MAX_CALL_DEPTH  32    /* Maximum function call depth */
#define SYN_WASM_MAX_FUNCTIONS   32    /* Max functions per WASM module */
#define SYN_WASM_MAX_HOST_FUNCS  16    /* Max registered host function callbacks */
#define SYN_WASM_MAX_GLOBALS    16    /* Max WASM global variables */

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
#include <syntropic/vm/syn_wasm.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static uint8_t wasm_ram[4096];
static SYN_WASM_Module mod;
static SYN_WASM_Context ctx;

/* Host function callback signature */
static uint64_t host_log_cb(SYN_WASM_Context *c, const uint64_t *args, uint8_t argc) {
    (void)c; (void)argc;
    printf("[WASM LOG] Code=%u, Val=%u\n", (uint32_t)args[0], (uint32_t)args[1]);
    return args[0] + args[1];
}

void run_wasm_app(const uint8_t *wasm_bytes, size_t wasm_size) {
    /* 1. Parse module header and sections from Flash */
    if (!syn_wasm_module_load(&mod, wasm_bytes, (uint32_t)wasm_size)) {
        printf("Error: Invalid WASM module\n");
        return;
    }

    /* 2. Initialize execution context with 4KB RAM buffer */
    if (!syn_wasm_init(&ctx, &mod, wasm_ram, sizeof(wasm_ram))) {
        printf("Error: WASM context init failed\n");
        return;
    }

    /* 3. Register native host callback at import index 0 */
    syn_wasm_register_host(&ctx, 0, host_log_cb);

    /* 4. Find exported function "run_tests" */
    int32_t fn_idx = syn_wasm_find_export(&mod, "run_tests");
    if (fn_idx < 0) {
        printf("Error: Exported function 'run_tests' not found\n");
        return;
    }

    /* 5. Set up call frame and execute with instruction slicing */
    syn_wasm_call(&ctx, (uint16_t)fn_idx);

    SYN_WASM_Status st;
    do {
        /* Slice execution: run up to 100 WASM opcodes per step */
        st = syn_wasm_step(&ctx, 100);
    } while (st == SYN_WASM_YIELDED);

    if (st == SYN_WASM_HALTED) {
        uint32_t result = (uint32_t)syn_wasm_result(&ctx);
        printf("WASM execution completed. Result: %u\n", result);
    } else {
        printf("WASM execution trapped! Trap code: %d\n", st);
    }
}

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Full register-level bare-metal driver implementation for CH32V307VCT6. Zero external HAL dependencies — direct peripheral register access.

Implemented peripherals: * SysTick / STK Timer (1ms system tick, microsecond clock, delay, reset) * GPIO (Ports A through E, set/reset/read/toggle) * USART (USART1..3 transmission and reception) * Flash (Fast Flash page erase and word programming) * SPI (SPI1 & SPI2 master full-duplex transfers) * I2C (I2C1 master read/write transactions) * CAN (CAN1 bxCAN-compatible frame transmission & reception) * ADC (ADC1 single-channel 12-bit conversions & DMA scan stubs) * EXTI (External pin interrupt configuration & masking)

/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 *  Global State
 * ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */

static volatile uint32_t s_tick_ms = 0U;
static volatile uint32_t s_critical_nesting = 0U;
static volatile uint32_t s_saved_mstatus = 0U;

#if defined(__riscv)
#define SYN_ISR_ATTR __attribute__((interrupt("machine")))
#else
#define SYN_ISR_ATTR
#endif

SYN_ISR_ATTR void SysTick_Handler(void)
{
#if defined(__riscv)
    uint32_t mstatus;
    __asm__ volatile("csrrci %0, mstatus, 8" : "=r"(mstatus)::"memory");
#endif
    s_tick_ms++;
    STK_SR = 0U;
#if defined(__riscv)
    if ((mstatus & 0x8U) != 0U) {
        __asm__ volatile("csrsi mstatus, 8" ::: "memory");
    }
#endif
}

/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 *  System & Clock Implementation
 * ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */

void syn_port_system_init(void)
{
    uint32_t reload = (uint32_t)(SYN_PORT_SYSCLK_HZ / 1000UL);
    if (reload > 0U) {
        reload -= 1U;
    }

    STK_CTLR = 0U;
    STK_SR = 0U;
    STK_CNTL = 0U;
    STK_CNTH = 0U;
    STK_CMPLR = reload;
    STK_CMPHR = 0U;
    STK_CTLR = STK_CTLR_INIT | STK_CTLR_STRE | STK_CTLR_STCLK | STK_CTLR_STIE | STK_CTLR_STE;

    syn_port_nvic_enable_irq(12U);
#if defined(__riscv)
    __asm__ volatile("csrsi mstatus, 8");
#endif
}

void syn_port_enter_critical(void)
{
    uint32_t mstatus = 0U;
#if defined(__riscv)
    __asm__ volatile("csrrci %0, mstatus, 8" : "=r"(mstatus)::"memory");
#endif
    if (s_critical_nesting == 0U) {
        s_saved_mstatus = mstatus;
    }
    s_critical_nesting++;
}

void syn_port_exit_critical(void)
{
#if defined(__riscv)
    __asm__ volatile("" ::: "memory");
#endif
    if (s_critical_nesting > 0U) {
        s_critical_nesting--;
        if (s_critical_nesting == 0U && (s_saved_mstatus & 0x8U) != 0U) {
#if defined(__riscv)
            __asm__ volatile("csrsi mstatus, 8" ::: "memory");
#endif
        }
    }
}

uint32_t syn_port_get_tick_ms(void)
{
    return s_tick_ms;
}

uint32_t syn_port_get_tick_us(void)
{
    uint32_t reload = STK_CMPLR;
    if ((STK_CTLR & STK_CTLR_STE) == 0U || reload == 0U || reload == UINT32_MAX) {
        return s_tick_ms * 1000U;
    }

    uint32_t ms1;
    uint32_t ms2;
    uint32_t cnt;
    uint32_t sr1;
    uint32_t sr2;
    do {
        ms1 = s_tick_ms;
        sr1 = STK_SR & STK_SR_CNTIF;
        cnt = STK_CNTL;
        ms2 = s_tick_ms;
        sr2 = STK_SR & STK_SR_CNTIF;
    } while (ms1 != ms2 || sr1 != sr2);

    if (sr1 != 0U) {
        ms1++;
        if (cnt >= reload) {
            cnt = 0U;
        }
    } else if (cnt > reload) {
        cnt = reload;
    }

    uint32_t elapsed_us = (uint32_t)(((uint64_t)cnt * 1000ULL) / ((uint64_t)reload + 1ULL));
    return (ms1 * 1000U) + elapsed_us;
}

void syn_port_delay_ms(uint32_t ms)
{
    uint32_t start = syn_port_get_tick_ms();
    while ((syn_port_get_tick_ms() - start) < ms) {
        __asm__ volatile("nop");
    }
}

void syn_port_nvic_set_priority(uint8_t irq_num, uint8_t preempt_prio, uint8_t sub_prio)
{
    /* QingKe V4F PFIC priority register base: 0xE000E000 + 0x400 + irq_num */
    volatile uint8_t *iprior = (volatile uint8_t *)0xE000E400UL;
    iprior[irq_num] = (uint8_t)((preempt_prio << 6) | (sub_prio << 4));
}

void syn_port_nvic_enable_irq(uint8_t irq_num)
{
    /* QingKe V4F PFIC enable register: 0xE000E100 */
    volatile uint32_t *ienr = (volatile uint32_t *)0xE000E100UL;
    ienr[irq_num >> 5] |= (1U << (irq_num & 0x1FU));
}

SYN_NORETURN void syn_port_system_reset(void)
{
    PFIC_CFGR = PFIC_CFGR_RESETSYS;
    while (1) {
    }
}

/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 *  GPIO Implementation
 * ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */

SYN_Status syn_port_gpio_init(SYN_GPIO_Pin pin, SYN_GPIO_Mode mode)
{
    uint32_t port_idx = pin >> 4;
    uint32_t pin_idx = pin & 0x0FU;

    if (port_idx >= NUM_GPIO_PORTS) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }

    RCC_APB2PCENR |= (1U << (port_idx + 2));

    GPIO_TypeDef *gpio = gpio_ports[port_idx];

    uint32_t config_val;
    switch (mode) {
    case SYN_GPIO_OUTPUT:
        config_val = 0x3U;
        break;
    case SYN_GPIO_OUTPUT_OD:
        config_val = 0x7U;
        break;
    case SYN_GPIO_INPUT_PULLUP:
        config_val = 0x8U;
        gpio->BSHR = (1U << pin_idx);
        break;
    case SYN_GPIO_INPUT_PULLDOWN:
        config_val = 0x8U;
        gpio->BCR = (1U << pin_idx);
        break;
    case SYN_GPIO_INPUT:
        config_val = 0x4U;
        break;
    default:
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }

    if (pin_idx < 8U) {
        uint32_t shift = pin_idx * 4U;
        gpio->CFGLR = (gpio->CFGLR & ~(0xFU << shift)) | (config_val << shift);
    } else {
        uint32_t shift = (pin_idx - 8U) * 4U;
        gpio->CFGHR = (gpio->CFGHR & ~(0xFU << shift)) | (config_val << shift);
    }

    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_gpio_deinit(SYN_GPIO_Pin pin)
{
    return syn_port_gpio_init(pin, SYN_GPIO_INPUT);
}

SYN_Status syn_port_gpio_write(SYN_GPIO_Pin pin, SYN_GPIO_State state)
{
    uint32_t port_idx = pin >> 4;
    uint32_t pin_idx = pin & 0x0FU;

    if (port_idx >= NUM_GPIO_PORTS) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }

    GPIO_TypeDef *gpio = gpio_ports[port_idx];
    if (state == SYN_GPIO_HIGH) {
        gpio->BSHR = (1U << pin_idx);
    } else {
        gpio->BCR = (1U << pin_idx);
    }

    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_GPIO_State syn_port_gpio_read(SYN_GPIO_Pin pin)
{
    uint32_t port_idx = pin >> 4;
    uint32_t pin_idx = pin & 0x0FU;

    if (port_idx >= NUM_GPIO_PORTS) {
        return SYN_GPIO_LOW;
    }

    GPIO_TypeDef *gpio = gpio_ports[port_idx];
    return (gpio->INDR & (1U << pin_idx)) ? SYN_GPIO_HIGH : SYN_GPIO_LOW;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_gpio_toggle(SYN_GPIO_Pin pin)
{
    SYN_GPIO_State curr = syn_port_gpio_read(pin);
    return syn_port_gpio_write(pin, (curr == SYN_GPIO_HIGH) ? SYN_GPIO_LOW : SYN_GPIO_HIGH);
}

/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 *  UART Implementation (USART1)
 * ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_init(SYN_UARTInstance instance, uint32_t baudrate)
{
    if (baudrate == 0U) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }
    if (instance != 0) {
        return SYN_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;
    }

    RCC_APB2PCENR |= RCC_USART1EN;

#ifndef SYN_PORT_SYSCLK_HZ
#define SYN_PORT_SYSCLK_HZ 144000000UL
#endif

    uint32_t pclk = SYN_PORT_SYSCLK_HZ;
    USART1->BRR = (pclk + baudrate / 2U) / baudrate;
    USART1->CTLR1 = USART_CTLR1_UE | USART_CTLR1_TE | USART_CTLR1_RE;

    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_deinit(SYN_UARTInstance instance)
{
    if (instance != 0)
        return SYN_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;
    USART1->CTLR1 = 0;
    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_transmit_byte(SYN_UARTInstance instance, uint8_t byte)
{
    if (instance != 0)
        return SYN_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;

    while (!(USART1->STATR & USART_STATR_TXE)) {
    }
    USART1->DATAR = byte;

    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_transmit(SYN_UARTInstance instance, const uint8_t *data, size_t len,
                                  uint32_t timeout_ms)
{
    (void)timeout_ms;
    if (data == NULL)
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;

    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        syn_port_uart_transmit_byte(instance, data[i]);
    }
    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_receive_byte(SYN_UARTInstance instance, uint8_t *byte, uint32_t timeout_ms)
{
    if (instance != 0 || byte == NULL) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }

    uint32_t start_ms = syn_port_get_tick_ms();
    do {
        if ((USART1->STATR & USART_STATR_RXNE) != 0U) {
            *byte = (uint8_t)USART1->DATAR;
            return SYN_OK;
        }
    } while ((syn_port_get_tick_ms() - start_ms) < timeout_ms);

    return SYN_TIMEOUT;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_uart_receive(SYN_UARTInstance instance, uint8_t *data, size_t len,
                                 size_t *received, uint32_t timeout_ms)
{
    if (instance != 0 || data == NULL || received == NULL) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }
    if (len == 0U) {
        *received = 0U;
        return SYN_OK;
    }

    size_t count = 0U;
    uint32_t start_ms = syn_port_get_tick_ms();
    while (count < len) {
        uint32_t elapsed = syn_port_get_tick_ms() - start_ms;
        uint32_t rem = (timeout_ms > elapsed) ? (timeout_ms - elapsed) : 0U;
        if (syn_port_uart_receive_byte(instance, &data[count], rem) == SYN_OK) {
            count++;
        } else {
            break;
        }
    }
    *received = count;
    return (count > 0U) ? SYN_OK : SYN_TIMEOUT;
}

int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len)
{
    (void)file;
    syn_port_uart_transmit(0, (const uint8_t *)ptr, (size_t)len, 100U);
    return len;
}

static SYN_Status ch32_flash_wait_bsy(void)
{
    volatile uint32_t timeout = 1000000UL;
    while ((FLASH_STATR & FLASH_STATR_BSY) != 0U && --timeout != 0UL) {
    }
    return (timeout > 0UL) ? SYN_OK : SYN_TIMEOUT;

SYN_Status syn_port_flash_read(uint32_t addr, void *buf, size_t len)
{
    if (len == 0U) {
        return SYN_OK;
    }
    if (buf == NULL) {

    return SYN_OK;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_flash_erase(uint32_t addr)
{
    if ((FLASH_CTLR & FLASH_CTLR_LOCK) != 0U) {
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY1;
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY2;
    }

    SYN_Status s = ch32_flash_wait_bsy();
    if (s != SYN_OK) {
        FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_LOCK;
        return s;
    }

    FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK | FLASH_STATR_EOP;
    FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_PER;
    FLASH_ADDR = addr;
    FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_STRT;

    s = ch32_flash_wait_bsy();
    if ((FLASH_STATR & FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK) != 0U) {
        FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK | FLASH_STATR_EOP;
        if (s == SYN_OK) {
            s = SYN_ERROR;
        }
    } else if ((FLASH_STATR & FLASH_STATR_EOP) != 0U) {
        FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_EOP;
    }

    FLASH_CTLR &= ~FLASH_CTLR_PER;
    FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_LOCK;

    return s;
}

SYN_Status syn_port_flash_write(uint32_t addr, const void *buf, size_t len)
{
    if (len == 0U) {
        return SYN_OK;
    }
    if (buf == NULL || (addr & 1U) != 0U) {
        return SYN_INVALID_PARAM;
    }

    if ((FLASH_CTLR & FLASH_CTLR_LOCK) != 0U) {
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY1;
        FLASH_KEYR = FLASH_KEY2;
    }

    SYN_Status s = ch32_flash_wait_bsy();
    if (s != SYN_OK) {
        FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_LOCK;
        return s;
    }

    FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK | FLASH_STATR_EOP;
    FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_PG;

    const uint8_t *src = (const uint8_t *)buf;
    for (size_t i = 0U; i < len; i += 2U) {
        uint16_t hw = (uint16_t)src[i];
        if ((i + 1U) < len) {
            hw |= (uint16_t)((uint16_t)src[i + 1U] << 8);
        } else {
            hw |= 0xFF00U;
        }
        *(volatile uint16_t *)(uintptr_t)(addr + (uint32_t)i) = hw;
        s = ch32_flash_wait_bsy();
        if (s != SYN_OK || (FLASH_STATR & FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK) != 0U) {
            FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_ERR_MASK | FLASH_STATR_EOP;
            FLASH_CTLR &= ~FLASH_CTLR_PG;
            FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_LOCK;
            return (s != SYN_OK) ? s : SYN_ERROR;
        }
        if ((FLASH_STATR & FLASH_STATR_EOP) != 0U) {
            FLASH_STATR = FLASH_STATR_EOP;
        }
    }

    FLASH_CTLR &= ~FLASH_CTLR_PG;
    FLASH_CTLR |= FLASH_CTLR_LOCK;
    return SYN_OK;
}

uint32_t syn_port_flash_sector_size(uint32_t addr)
{
    (void)addr;
    return 4U * 1024U;
}

{

        return SYN_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;

    for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        uint8_t send_val = tx ? tx[i] : 0xFFU;

        while (!(SPI1->STATR & SPI_STATR_TXE)) {
        }

        while (!(SPI1->STATR & SPI_STATR_RXNE)) {
        }

        if (rx) {
            rx[i] = recv_val;

    }

                             uint16_t own_addr)

        return SYN_NOT_IMPLEMENTED;
